own_scenes.desc: Stax era un negocio familiar en un viejo cine de Memphis, de dueños blancos (Jim Stewart y Estelle Axton) con una banda de estudio integrada (Steve Cropper, Isaac Hayes, Al Jackson, Duck Dunn, Booker T.) y solo artistas negros: ritmo pesado y vientos ásperos. Jerry Wexler llevó allí a Wilson Pickett, bailó el Jerk para enseñar el contratiempo de «In the Midnight Hour» y, cuando Stax lo vetó, lo llevó a los FAME de Rick Hall en Muscle Shoals, donde acababan de grabar «When a Man Loves a Woman» de Percy Sledge. Con una banda casi toda blanca (Spooner Oldham, Roger Hawkins) y pastillas, Pickett convirtió un estándar de cuatro años en la versión definitiva de «Land of 1000 Dances» (julio de 1966): gritos afinados, ritmo frenético, el «na, na-ne-na-na», un fragmento de un show que podría durar horas; parte de un continuo de la cultura negra entre el orgullo y la rabia. Otis Redding, heredero de Sam Cooke tras su asesinato, rompió con «I’ve Been Loving You Too Long» y Otis Blue fijó la palabra «soul», pero Stax no vendía como Motown hasta que Sam & Dave triunfaron con «Hold On! I’m Comin’». Los Beatles quisieron grabar en Stax en abril de 1966; su sonido está por todo Rubber Soul. La revista de Stax en Watts coincidió con los disturbios de agosto de 1965.

refs.q: Nothing quite like ‘Land of 1000 Dances’ had been heard before.
refs.para: Nothing quite like ‘Land of 1000 Dances’ had been heard before. The music licks along at an incredible pace, the cyclical guitar riff counterpointed against the explosive horns. Pickett drives this instrumental intensity with vocal interjections and gospel exhortations: he grunts, he screams, and hits at top speed the first ‘na, na-ne-na-na’ section that was the song’s hook. His voice is there not so much to convey the lyric – a series of dance-floor attitudes – but to be an integral part of the rhythm.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: Stax was a small, family-owned business operating from an old cinema in downtown Memphis.
refs.para: Stax was a small, family-owned business operating from an old cinema in downtown Memphis. The old lobby was a record shop, Satellite, and the main hall was converted into a small studio that was open day and night. Although owned by whites – Jim Stewart and his sister, Estelle Axton – Stax ran an integrated house band – which featured, among others, Steve Cropper, Isaac Hayes, Al Jackson, Duck Dunn and Booker T. – and promoted exclusively black American performers.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: Explosive, compressed, ecstatic, Pickett’s ‘Land of 1000 Dances’ was faster than any other dance tune of the time.
refs.para: Explosive, compressed, ecstatic, Pickett’s ‘Land of 1000 Dances’ was faster than any other dance tune of the time. Bucking and leaping like a wild mustang, it had an immediate impact upon its release in mid-July 1966, hitting radio playlists and the Billboard Top 60 by the end of the month. It was one of those records that, through its very force, pulled the culture along with it, ratcheting up the intensity, matching and pushing the changing rhythms of the dances.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: But the Stax breakthrough came with Sam and Dave’s ‘Hold On! I’m Coming’.
refs.para: But the Stax breakthrough came with Sam and Dave’s ‘Hold On! I’m Coming’. Writers Dave Porter and Isaac Hayes studied the Motown narrative template – in particular, Smokey Robinson’s lyric for the Temptations’ ‘Don’t Look Back’ – and decided to throw in a bit of James Brown and Lee Dorsey. It reached #21 in mid-June. ‘That’s when the thought processes really started working,’ Porter told Rob Bowman, ‘and an identity started taking place.’
